newsitem.title: UK: POLL-19/20 analysts see UK rates unchanged this wk. [CORRECTED 17:25 GMT]
newsitem.headline: POLL-19/20 analysts see UK rates unchanged this wk. [CORRECTED 17:25 GMT]

text.p: UK Chancellor Kenneth Clarke will keep base rates on hold at 5.75 percent when he meets the Bank of England Governor Eddie George on Wednesday, a Reuters poll showed on Monday.
Economists surveyed said subdued inflationary pressure combined with strong sterling would help Clarke resist pressure from the governor to raise rates.
"There's going to be a less than explosive recovery accompanied by few obvious signs of price pressure...all reasons for Clarke not to raise rates," said Alex Garrard, UK economist at UBS.
Sterling has appreciated over 6-1/2 percent since the beginning of August and this rally would give the chancellor additional resistance to George's push for higher rates.
A crude rule of thumb suggests that a four percent appreciation in sterling is equivalent to a one percent increase in base rates, economists say.
But with Clarke widely predicted to ease fiscal policy with modest tax give-aways in November 26's budget, economists felt he would hold fire on monetary policy until he could gauge market reaction.

Nineteen of the 20 economists polled said rates would stick at current levels, before an incoming government tightened policy by an average of 50 basis points after a general election, expected in May 1997.

But four economists reckoned a manufacturing pickup and sustained pressure from Eddie George would mean Clarke would succumb and put rates up before an election. This included Richard Jeffrey, group economist at Charterhouse, the only economist to predict a base rate change this Wednesday.

"Inflation signals have been deteriorating, we've got pretty strong domestic demand and I think if Clarke feels that a tightening is going to be appropriate in any stage before an election it's better to get it out of the way," Jeffrey said.
Kevin Gardiner, UK economist at Morgan Stanley agreed, although he did not expect rates to rise until the beginning of next year.

"The economic argument will be so powerful that for the chancellor to over-rule such technocratic advice from the Bank of England would risk a political backlash," he said. "I dont think he'd do that - he's too astute a politician to risk giving the opposition and the media such an open goal".
Only Andrew Davies at London Bond Broking reckoned Clarke would have the nerve to sneak in one last cut before the election.

"If he produces a budget which is well received by the markets and maintains sterling's level on the foreign exchanges, he could argue that monetary policy had in fact been tightened and there was therefore a scope for a reduction in rates," Davies said.
The poll predicted that rates would rise to an average of 7.0 percent in 1997, although some economists said monetary tightening could see base rates as high as 9.0 percent in 1998.
